title: Millions of Kids Now Have Trump Accounts, but New Rules Raise Questions
summary:
The U.S. Treasury Department has created Trump Accounts for every eligible child in the country. More than 60 million children were enrolled automatically. That adds to about seven million children whose parents had already signed them up since the program started in July.

A Trump Account is an investment account for a child. Over time it turns into an IRA, which is a kind of savings account for retirement. The idea is that money put in while a child is young can grow for many years.

The expansion also came with new rules. Under the original plan written by Congress, money in the accounts went into low-cost index funds. An index fund holds small pieces of many companies at once. Money from parents and employers still goes into those funds.

Now, however, donors can also give individual stocks, which are shares in a single company. Families cannot choose or reject these stocks, and they must keep them for five years. Donors can also aim gifts at certain groups of children, based on where they live or how old they are. All donated money must go through a nonprofit, and the Treasury Department must approve it.

Wall Street Journal reporter Richard Rubin told PBS NewsHour that the changes are totally different from the first plan. He said many people expect wealthy individuals to make these gifts. Michael Dell and his wife, Susan, have already given more than $6 billion in cash.

The Treasury Department says the changes will encourage more donors to give and help families feel invested in companies. It also says automatic enrollment helps children from lower-income families, who may not have signed up on their own. Rubin said data supports that idea. He also said some experts have raised concerns about the stock rules.
why_it_matters: The program puts money for the future in the names of tens of millions of children, and the new rules change who decides how that money is invested.
